# Summary: Bivariate Analysis of Workforce Participation Outcomes Among Non-College Completers The bivariate analysis examined associations between 21 independent variables and workforce participation outcomes at years 1, 5, and 10 post-graduation among Southwest Minnesota high school graduates who did not complete a postsecondary credential. Variables are ranked separately for categorical predictors (Cramer's V) and continuous predictors (F-statistic from ANOVA) given the absence of a common effect size metric across the two approaches. Rankings reflect general patterns across all three time points, with particular attention to consistency and magnitude of effect. ## **Categorical Predictors Ranked by Effect Size (Cramer's V)** *1. Postsecondary Attendance* (V=0.640, 0.275, 0.124) is the strongest categorical predictor by a substantial margin, though the year 1 association is largely structural — driven by the mechanical relationship between attending postsecondary and the attending ps outcome category. Its most substantive and durable finding is that postsecondary attendees show persistently higher sustained statewide employment and lower regional employment relative to non-attendees across all three time points, consistent with the academic pathway. *2. ACT Participation* (V=0.302, 0.155, 0.108) is the strongest high school accomplishment predictor and the strongest variable with a clearly substantive rather than structural association at year 1. Its signature — higher postsecondary attendance, lower regional employment, and substantially higher statewide employment — is the clearest expression of the academic pathway among non-college completers and remains the second strongest categorical predictor at every time point. *3. AP Exam Participation* (V=0.149, 0.101, 0.065) ranks third, producing a pattern nearly identical to ACT participation in character — high postsecondary attendance early, persistently lower regional and higher statewide employment — but with smaller effect sizes throughout and greater attenuation by year 10. *4. PSEO Participation* (V=0.186, 0.072, 0.082) ranks fourth overall, with a strong year 1 association driven by an 18-percentage-point postsecondary attendance gap that dissipates rapidly. Its residual finding — a persistent tendency toward statewide rather than regional employment among PSEO participants who did not complete — mirrors the broader academic pathway pattern but at modest effect sizes at years 5 and 10. Note that this variable is restricted to 2011 cohorts and later. *5. Special Education Status* (V=0.171, 0.107, 0.093) is the strongest demographic predictor, distinguished from other demographic variables by its persistent association with employment instability and reduced statewide labor market mobility across all three time points. Its primary signature is not reduced regional employment but rather elevated non-sustained workforce participation and lower statewide employment that endure through year 10. *6. English Learner Status* (V=0.140, 0.074, 0.070) ranks sixth, with a strong year 1 association reflecting lower postsecondary attendance and a persistent and growing absence from Minnesota employment records that is its most distinctive feature — differentiating it from other demographic variables and suggesting out-of-state employment, informal work, or geographic departure as plausible explanations. *7. Economic Status* (V=0.137, 0.083, 0.091) ranks seventh, with a strong year 1 association again driven largely by differential postsecondary attendance. Its most durable finding is modestly higher sustained statewide employment among non-disadvantaged graduates and greater employment instability among disadvantaged graduates, though the association weakens considerably from year 1 to year 5. *8. CTE Achievement* (V=0.094, 0.106, 0.115) is notable as the only accomplishments variable whose effect size grows at every time point, and the strongest categorical predictor oriented toward regional rather than statewide employment. CTE concentrators and completers show progressively higher regional employment and lower no MN employment record rates relative to the no CTE group, with a 15-percentage-point regional employment gap emerging by year 10. *9. Non-English Home Language* (V=0.114, 0.068, 0.061) ranks ninth, closely mirroring the English learner pattern in both direction and character but with consistently smaller effect sizes, suggesting that English learner status captures the relevant variation more precisely. Its independent contribution will require evaluation in multivariate models. *10. EDR* (V=0.093, 0.103, 0.107) is the strongest high school characteristics predictor, with a growing association driven primarily by a widening gap in sustained statewide employment between EDR 6E (Southwest Central) and the other two EDRs — a geographic labor market differentiation that is largely invisible in the regional employment category, which is similar across all three EDRs. *11. Gender* (V=0.058, 0.087, 0.107) ranks eleventh and is distinctive as the only variable whose effect size increases consistently across all three time points. Its growing association reflects a widening gap in sustained regional employment favoring males and an expanding share of females carrying no MN employment record by year 10, suggesting diverging long-term labor market trajectories by gender. *12. Race/Ethnicity* (V=0.069, 0.043, 0.054) shows the weakest and least consistent effect sizes of the categorical variables, with American Indian graduates showing a persistently adverse profile and Asian/Pacific Islander graduates displaying a distinctive pattern of high MN record absence alongside relatively high statewide employment among those who remain. Overall effect sizes are small at all three time points. *13. Community Demographic Description* (V=0.054, 0.078, 0.094) shows statistically significant but practically weak associations, with the most interpretable pattern being a growing statewide employment advantage for urban/town/rural mix graduates and higher MN record absence among entirely rural graduates. Effect sizes remain too small to add meaningful explanatory value beyond other variables. ## **Continuous Predictors Ranked by Effect Size (F-statistic)** *1. Total CTE Courses Taken* (F=146.8, 101.3, 62.1) produces the highest F-statistics of any continuous variable at all three time points. Its pattern is the mirror image of the academic achievement variables: higher CTE course volume is strongly and consistently associated with sustained regional employment, while the no MN employment record group shows persistently the lowest CTE course-taking at every observation window. The three-tier structure at year 10 — regional employment highest, statewide and non-sustained in the middle, no MN record lowest — is among the clearest patterns in the entire analysis. *2. MCA Reading Score* (F=144.3, 42.0, 28.0) is the strongest academic achievement measure, consistent with its role as the primary achievement indicator in the full population multivariate models. Its gradient is clear and durable across all three time points: higher scores are associated with statewide employment and — increasingly over time — no MN employment record, while regional employment and non-sustained work form the lowest-scoring tier. F-statistics are the highest of the three MCA measures at years 1 and 5. *3. ACT Composite Score* (F=114.2, 44.6, 18.3) ranks third among continuous predictors, producing a pattern consistent with MCA Reading: higher scores associated with postsecondary attendance early and statewide employment later, with regional employment consistently at the lowest-scoring tier. The score gap between sustained statewide and sustained regional employment grows from 0.79 points at year 1 to 1.43 points at year 10, indicating increasing score-based stratification across the observation windows. Note this variable is restricted to ACT takers only. *4. MCA Math Score* (F=89.4, 36.0, 34.6) closely mirrors MCA Reading in pattern but with somewhat lower F-statistics at years 1 and 5. Its year 10 F-statistic (34.6) exceeds MCA Reading (28.0), suggesting math achievement carries slightly stronger differentiation at the later time point. The three-tier consolidation at year 10 — statewide and no MN record as a higher-achieving group, regional and non-sustained as a lower-achieving group — replicates the MCA Reading structure. *5. MCA Science Score* (F=84.4, 38.1, 25.1) replicates the MCA Reading and Math patterns with high fidelity across all three time points, including the three-tier consolidation at year 10. As in the full population analysis, its voluntary and self-selected nature limits its utility in multivariate models, but its bivariate associations confirm the broader academic achievement gradient and are consistent with retaining MCA Reading as the primary academic achievement indicator. *6. Average County Unemployment Rate* (F=31.3, 44.5, 54.7) is notable as the only continuous variable whose F-statistic increases substantially over time, reflecting a growing labor market geography effect. Its most consistent finding is that graduates achieving sustained statewide employment disproportionately originate from higher-unemployment counties — consistent with a labor market push dynamic — while the no MN employment record group shows unemployment rate profiles indistinguishable from sustained regional workers, suggesting out-of-state departure rather than intra-state mobility. *7. Average County Wages as Percent of State Average* (F=35.3, 24.0, 26.1) is statistically significant at all three time points but shows very small absolute differences — all contrasts within one to two percentage points of the state average. Its only durable finding mirrors the unemployment rate variable: graduates in sustained statewide employment consistently originate from lower-wage counties. The negligible absolute magnitude of differences limits its practical significance and supports its exclusion from multivariate models. ## **Cross-Cutting Observations** Several themes emerge from the full set of bivariate findings. First, the two-pathway structure identified in the full population analysis is fully present among non-college completers: academic indicators (ACT, AP, PSEO, MCA scores, postsecondary attendance) consistently predict statewide labor market mobility, while CTE indicators (CTE achievement, total CTE courses) predict regional attachment — regardless of whether a credential was earned. Second, the no MN employment record category behaves distinctively across the accomplishment variables, increasingly resembling the statewide employment group on academic achievement measures by years 5 and 10, suggesting that a meaningful share of higher-achieving non-completers have left Minnesota rather than failing to engage with its labor market. Third, demographic variables show weaker associations than accomplishment variables across the board, indicating that what students did in high school is more predictive of workforce participation trajectories than who they are. Finally, several variables — community demographic description, county wages, non-English home language — show statistically significant but practically weak associations unlikely to add explanatory value beyond stronger correlated predictors in multivariate models, consistent with decisions made in the full population analysis.
# What the Data Tell Us: Workforce Participation Among Non-College Completers For Southwest Minnesota high school graduates who never earned a postsecondary credential, the years following graduation tell two very different stories depending on the path they took through high school. ## **The students who were headed somewhere else** Some graduates who ultimately did not complete a postsecondary credential were nonetheless oriented toward college from the start. They took the ACT, participated in AP courses and PSEO, earned higher MCA scores, and went on to attempt postsecondary education even if they didn't finish it. What happened to them in the labor market looks a lot like what happened to students who did complete degrees — just a dimmer version of the same pattern. They were more likely to leave Southwest Minnesota for employment elsewhere in the state, and by year 10, a striking share of them had simply disappeared from Minnesota employment records entirely. They weren't failing to find work. The most likely explanation is that they left the state. This group illustrates something important: academic orientation shapes where people end up even when formal credentials don't follow. The habits of mind, the networks, the postsecondary experience itself — even an incomplete one — appear to pull people toward broader labor markets and away from the region. ## **The students who were built for this place** The other story belongs to graduates with deep CTE engagement. Higher numbers of CTE courses taken, CTE concentrator or completer status — these are the students who showed up in regional employment at year 1 and stayed there. By year 10, CTE concentrators were nearly twice as likely to be in sustained regional employment as graduates with no CTE engagement at all. This isn't a small finding. It suggests that CTE programs are doing exactly what they are supposed to do for students who engage with them seriously: connecting young people to the regional economy and equipping them to stay. ## **The students who fell through the cracks** The most troubling pattern in the data belongs to graduates with no CTE engagement and no academic orientation — the students who neither pursued a college track nor developed occupational skills through CTE. By year 10, more than half of graduates with no CTE participation carried no Minnesota employment record at all. This group was already the most likely to have no MN employment record at year 1, and that gap only widened over time. Whether they left the state, work in informal economies, or have simply disengaged from the formal labor market, the data cannot say — but their persistent absence from employment records across a decade is the most concerning finding in the entire analysis. ## **The role of identity and circumstance** Demographic characteristics — race, gender, economic status, special education status, English learner status — do matter, but they matter less than what students did in high school. Special education students show persistent employment instability. English learners and graduates from non-English speaking homes show elevated absence from Minnesota employment records that grows over time, possibly reflecting employment in sectors that don't generate wage records or communities that maintain strong ties outside Minnesota. Males are more likely to be in sustained regional employment by year 10; females are increasingly likely to carry no MN employment record. These patterns deserve attention, but they operate in the background of the stronger story told by high school experiences. ## **The geography of opportunity** Where a student went to high school also matters, though modestly. Graduates from EDR 6E — the Southwest Central region anchored by Marshall — show substantially higher rates of employment outside the region compared to graduates from the Upper Minnesota Valley or Southwest EDRs. Graduates from higher- unemployment counties are more likely to leave the region for work elsewhere in the state, consistent with what we would expect when local job markets are tight. But sustained regional employment rates are remarkably similar across the three EDRs, suggesting that the regional economy absorbs similar shares of non-completers regardless of sub-region — it's the path out of the region that differs. ## **The bottom line** A decade after high school graduation, the non-college completer population has sorted into roughly three groups: those doing steady work in the region, those doing steady work elsewhere, and a large and growing group with no formal Minnesota employment footprint. CTE engagement is the strongest predictor of being in the first group. Academic orientation — even without a credential — predicts the second. And the absence of either, combined with demographic disadvantage, is the clearest signal of the third. The regional economy depends heavily on workers who choose to stay. This analysis suggests that CTE programs are the most powerful mechanism available for cultivating that attachment among students who will not complete four-year degrees. At the same time, the growing share of non-completers absent from Minnesota employment records by year 10 — many of them higher-achieving graduates who attended postsecondary without finishing — points to an ongoing and unresolved challenge: how to keep talent in a region when the pathways that develop it often point toward somewhere else.
